A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
LTIIb binds specifically to Y1 tissue cells and mouse intestinal epithelial cells, and that LTIIa inhibits the binding of class I and LT-IIb toxins.
LTIIb, like LTI, binds to gangliosides, but that the ganglioside receptor for LTIIb is different from that of LTI.

the B subunits of the class I toxins have a greater affinity for ganglioside GM1 than the LTII B subunits, and the B subunits from both class II LTs can inhibit the activity of cholera enterotoxins, but only the B subunit from LTIIb can inhibit the activity or the binding of LTIIb.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the class II LTs, LTIIa and LTIIb, are not recognized by the receptors of the class I toxins, cholera toxin (CT) and LTI.
class II toxins have a unique receptor specificity which is different from that of class I and other enterotoxines.
LTIIb binds to mouse Y1 cells and intestinal cells in a manner similar to LTI and cholera enterotoxins, but unlike LTIIa.
